summary: The English of all six mishnayot is faithful, brief and consistent with Bartenura and Rambam; no reading needs to change. The main fault is in the senses: many were filled from whatever entry the pack linked, so they name a place or person (Tob, Helek, Sacar, Tikvah, Enos, Shem, Ramah, Atarah), a verb for a noun, or BDB's 'law (of man)' for the Torah; these are moved to the right Jastrow entries or removed. Smaller errors: אֶרֶךְ (Prov 16:32) is the adjective אָרֵךְ, not the noun; לָךְ of Ps 128:2 is masculine pausal, not feminine; בָז is the participle of בוז; two commentary summaries and one apparatus line misreport their source. The model morphology has the same errors (אֶרֶךְ, לָךְ twice, בָז) and an absolute for the emphatic תָּגָא.

value: The saying has four parallel questions, each introduced by אֵיזֶהוּ ('who is it that...?') and answered by a participle with the article (הַלּוֹמֵד, הַכּוֹבֵשׁ, הַשָּׂמֵחַ, הַמְכַבֵּד): 'the one who learns', 'the one who subdues'. The participle with the article serves as a relative clause.

Each answer is closed by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ('as it is said') and a verse from the Bible; the verses are quoted in their biblical form, so Psalm 119 and 128 address God and the hearer directly, with biblical forms (עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ; לָךְ, the pausal form of the masculine לְךָ) that are not mishnaic Hebrew.

Proverbs 16:32 is built on מִ of comparison, doubled: טוֹב אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם מִגִּבּוֹר וּמֹשֵׁל בְּרוּחוֹ מִלֹּכֵד עִיר, 'better the slow-of-anger than the hero, and the ruler over his spirit than the taker of a city'.

Psalm 128:2: אַשְׁרֶיךָ is a plural construct noun used as an exclamation ('happy are you'). The mishnah splits the verse in two and gives a time to each half: 'in this world' for אַשְׁרֶיךָ and 'in the world to come' for טוֹב לָךְ.

1 Samuel 2:30 pairs a Piel participle (מְכַבְּדַי) with the matching Piel imperfect (אֲכַבֵּד); the verb root כבד has the sense 'be heavy' and the Piel 'give weight to, honor'. The same root underlies מְכֻבָּד (Pual), 'honored'. יֵקָלּוּ 'will be light' is the opposite of 'heavy'.
patches.reason: לָךְ in Ps 128:2 is the masculine pausal form, not a 2nd feminine ending.

patches.value: Rambam: 'this is clear, and we already mentioned its matter in the preceding chapters'. The comment is on the whole mishnah (its DH is the word זה 'this' of his own sentence), not on הַזֶּה; it adds nothing to the English.
patches.reason: The old summary added an explanation Rambam does not give ('the contrast between this world and the world to come') and took his זה for the mishnah's הַזֶּה.

patches.value: Rabbeinu Yonah: an 'erekh appayim' is one who holds back his anger and does not want to take revenge at once, but waits for a time and a place to take it; the hot-tempered man who avenges himself at once spoils his deeds and acts without understanding. A moral gloss, not a reading of the words.
patches.reason: The clause on the one who rules his spirit and forgives from fear of God is in 4:1:6, not 4:1:5; and 4:1:5 also says why quick revenge is bad.

value: הֱוֵי is an imperative of 'be' (an Aramaic-style form common in the sayings); with the participle רָץ it means 'be running', i.e. 'run'. The two commands are parallel: 'run to...' and 'flee from...' (בּוֹרֵחַ is also a participle).
קַלָּה and חֲמוּרָה are feminine adjectives agreeing with מִצְוָה; the second is used alone with כְּ + בְּ: 'as to a weighty one'.

The reasons come in two clauses with שֶׁ ('for'), each a pair of short sentences: 'a commandment draws a commandment, and a transgression draws a transgression'; 'the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression'. The second pair has no verb 'is': the two nouns are placed side by side.
גּוֹרֶרֶת is a feminine participle of גרר, literally 'drag' (Jastrow 3), here 'draw along, bring after it'.
patches.reason: There are two שֶׁ clauses (שֶׁמִּצְוָה, שֶׁשְּׂכַר), not three; and only the second pair lacks a verb (the first has גּוֹרֶרֶת).

patches.value: בָז is the Qal participle of the hollow verb בּוּז 'despise' (not of בזה, and not an adjective): 'one who despises'. With תְּהִי: 'be one who despises'. No entry in the supplied lexicon.
patches.reason: בָּז is the participle of בוז; the note called it an adjective.

value: Rabbeinu Yonah's own text (4:5:1) reads 'Rabbi Shimon his son'; the editor's bracket in it notes that our text reads 'Rabbi Ishmael'. The base text here has Rabbi Ishmael.

Vilna spelling variants: ללמוד (4:5.12, 4:5.20), לשמור (4:5.22), קרדום (4:5.33), לחפור (4:5.34), ודישתמש (4:5.40, for the base וּדְאִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ); the pack also shows that Vilna has no word at 4:5.6 where the base has תּוֹרָה.
Bartenura's variant text: 'one who learns in order to teach: they do not enable him to learn and to teach' (taking לְלַמֵּד as 'in order to be called Rabbi'); he follows the reading in most books.
patches.reason: The attribution was reversed: Rabbeinu Yonah's DH reads רבי (שמעון בנו), and it is the copyist/editor (אמר המעתיק) who notes that 'before us' the reading is Rabbi Ishmael.
אֶרֶךְ is the construct of the adjective אָרֵךְ 'long' (BDB s.v. אָרֵךְ: cstr. אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם); the noun אֹרֶךְ keeps its holam in the construct (Prov 25:15).
לָךְ in pause is the masculine לְךָ; Ps 128:2 addresses a man (כַּפֶּיךָ, תֹאכֵל, אַשְׁרֶיךָ).
The verse's masculine pausal לָךְ, quoted again; not feminine.

patches.reason: בָּז is the Qal participle of the hollow root בוז 'despise' (cf. Prov 13:13 בָּז לְדָבָר), not an adjective of בזה.
תָּגָא is in the Aramaic emphatic (determined) state, 'the crown', not the absolute (תָּג).

verdicts.comment: Bartenura reads the min of מִגִּבּוֹר and מִלֹּכֵד as 'coming from' (patience that comes from might; ruling one's spirit after taking a city). The English keeps the plain comparative of Prov 16:32, which is what the mishnah's proof needs ('better than a hero'); Rambam does not comment, so there is no agreement of the two normative commentators against it, and the reading is recorded.
A general remark that the mishnah is clear.
The English keeps the plain saying, which admits his reading.
The English keeps 'from the world'; Rambam's 'from the life of the world to come' is in the note and the phrase literal.
